title: AI Brief Hub — Week of October 26, 2026
headline: Cheaper frontier models, phone-native agents and lab-tested AI science let one person build, create and discover at team scale.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Andrej Karpathy built a video site in about two hours. Claude Code did the work. More than six thousand videos, distilled from forty-three million Hacker News comments. And that's the warm-up. A hobbyist says Claude booked robotic telescopes in Chile, Spain and Utah, then sent asteroid positions to the Minor Planet Center. Plus a solar-cell result that narrowed ninety thousand candidate molecules down to three hundred. It was a full week. From the AI Brief Hub, I'm Jordan Reeves. Let's get into it.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Priya, that Karpathy build ate the timeline all week. Where do you want to start?

segments.speaker: x_correspondent
segments.text: With the two hours, Jordan. Two hours.

segments.speaker: x_correspondent
segments.text:
Andrej Karpathy had Claude Code read twenty years of Hacker News comments and pull out the videos people keep recommending. Six thousand, four hundred fifty-four of them. Then deploy a no-login viewing site called HackerTube. Opus five point five, medium effort. The post pulled more than two million views, and the data ships as a zip, so anyone can point their own Claude at it and make a version. Steal this idea: swap a feed you hate for one built from a community's comment history. Take twenty years of posts from a forum your engineers read and have an agent surface the papers and links people keep recommending.

Next. Pieter Levels dropped raw DJI clips into a folder and opened Claude Code in it. Asked for a ten-minute vlog. It transcribed his speech with a Whisper model and cut the edit. He says he made only a few adjustments. Greg Isenberg called it the moment anyone can run a video marketing machine without a team. Wild. Same pattern as Karpathy's: one folder, one agent, one finished thing. Steal this idea: record a quick walkthrough of a prototype or a lab setup, and ask the agent for a captioned two-minute update.

And the one with the biggest crowd. ChatGPT now lets Pro users in the US text their personal agent, the Dot, over iMessage or RCS. Hand it a task. Send a photo or a voice note. Ask it to keep watch on something, and it texts you back on its own with updates. A preview, rolling out now, and more than three million views. People want an agent they reach the way they reach a coworker. Steal this idea: text it a photo of something you need figured out, and ask for a follow-up tomorrow. That's the timeline. Over to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: From the timeline to the night sky. Sam, show us the telescopes.

segments.speaker: reddit_correspondent
segments.text:
Reddit this week had a hobbyist with a robot astronomer. A poster on the Claude subreddit lets Claude pick targets, check where the Moon is, and set filters and exposures. It books time on rented robotic telescopes in Chile, Spain and Utah. Then it downloads the frames and stacks them. Three nights in, the poster reports fifty-seven positions of eight asteroids sent to the Minor Planet Center, plus finished shots of the Helix Nebula, Orion and the Tarantula. More than fifteen hundred upvotes. And look, this is the part the demo reels skip: a full plan, book, collect and process loop on hardware nobody in the thread owns. Steal this idea: pick any remote instrument you can rent by the hour, a test rig, a camera, a lab service, and let an agent run one night of it.

Same subreddit, similar trick. A builder made openskycam, an open-source sky camera that records in four-K around the clock on his own disk and exposes every action through an MCP server. That's the Model Context Protocol, the standard plug that lets an agent drive a tool. The builder says Claude Code built the nightly workflow and sorted seventeen meteors from Saturday night before he woke up. Fourteen hundred upvotes. Steal this idea: give any sensor you own an MCP server and let an agent be the night-shift reviewer. Ask for a morning digest of what moved.

Now something just for fun. Free browser games turn two to four phones on a table into one shared board. The phones find each other over the same Wi-Fi or a four-letter code, and a puck can slide right off one screen onto the next. Ten games so far. Air hockey, hot potato, a snake game for up to twelve players. Eighteen hundred upvotes. Steal this idea: line up every spare tablet at a trade-show booth and make one giant display.

One for the scientists. C and E N reports a UT Dallas chemistry professor, Jeremiah Gassensmith, vibe coded ChemDraft, a free replacement for ChemDraw, the structure-drawing tool chemists have used for decades. One commenter says they built their own version two weeks earlier, in about four iterations. Steal this idea: ask your lab which paid tool they'd replace first, and let one researcher try it over a weekend. That's the show-and-tell. Jordan, back to you.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Priya and Sam both showed one person doing the work of a crew. Marcus, the YouTube builders went even further. Who's making money?

segments.speaker: youtube_correspondent
segments.text:
Okay so — start with a founder story. Broccoli, on the YC Root Access channel. The founders say their AI front office for home-services businesses went from zero to an expected sixty million dollars in annual recurring revenue in two years. It answers calls, follows up on leads and books appointments across voice and text for more than five hundred customers. And here's the move: they visited a hundred forty contractors first to find the real problem. YC says the booked-job run rate for those customers tops a billion dollars a year. One unglamorous job, done perfectly. Steal this idea: pick the phone line nobody loves, like dispatch or quoting. Give it a voice agent that books straight into the calendar. Count booked jobs, not call minutes.

Second, if you want numbers, Nick Saraev ran GPT-six point one Terra in Codex against Claude Opus five point five in Claude Code, same prompts. Terra finished builds in twenty-three minutes forty-three seconds on average. Opus took forty-three minutes fifty-two. He tests a game, a landing page, a Minecraft-style build, computer use and vision, then tells you when to reach for each. OpenAI lists Terra at one dollar per million input tokens and five dollars per million output. Steal this idea: run your own three favorite tasks through both and keep a scoreboard for the next launch.

Third, the pure fun one. Skill Leap AI has Claude build three 3D worlds with Blender and Unreal Engine, on a laptop with a Claude subscription, first prompt to finished scene. The pitch: people who've never touched either tool can stage game worlds by describing them. Steal this idea: describe a product in a room, or a facility layout, and get a walkable draft by the end of a meeting. The through-line this week, one person, one tool, one real result. That's YouTube. The mic is yours, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Marcus had Claude building 3D worlds. Maya, the repos this week go a step further. One turns a single AI video into a rigged 3D character.

segments.speaker: builders_correspondent
segments.text:
Builders this week. Three repos, none of them frameworks. All of them things you can use tonight. First, anymove, the one Jordan just teased. It turns one AI-generated video of a creature into a rigged 3D animation. Two camera views sit in a single frame to pin every joint, the rig is fitted frame by frame, and it exports a GLB file. The maker puts a usable move at about three dollars all in. Examples include a dragon, a giant spider and a wolf. Apache licensed, four hundred sixty stars in its first days. What it lets you do: use a video model as a cheap motion-capture studio. Steal this idea: film a mechanism with a video model from two angles and see if the same trick gives you a motion path for a demo.

Second, Mika. Priya covered texting your Dot. Mika is the other road. It's an on-device Android agent. Give it a sentence and it works your apps and the web on a hidden background screen while you keep using the phone. About thirty-nine hundred stars in three days. The README demos show price-capped shopping, flight lookups and job-site outreach. Steal this idea: hand it one recurring errand, comparing prices or checking a feed, and time it against yourself.

Third, pixelfx. A free library of two hundred forty-four pixel-art effects: fire, weather, pickups, chained attack moves. Plus a Claude Code skill that draws a new effect, looks at it, and refines it. Over twenty-five hundred stars in its first two days. The clever part is treating art as code the agent can render and judge by eye, so craft ships as a reusable skill. Steal this idea: write a skill for your own house style, slide diagrams or product renders, and ask for ten variations before lunch. That's the toolbox, and it's back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Speaking of shipping, Diego, what actually launched?

segments.speaker: launches_correspondent
segments.text:
Five launches, five different buyers. First, a frontier model for the person with a long to-do list. Google says Gemini four Carbon ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, version five, with a score of fifty-nine, and it's built for long-running agent work. Launch pricing is two dollars per million input tokens and ten per million output, rising to four and twenty after the introductory period. Access starts with a subset of cyber defenders and trusted partners, with developers, businesses and consumers to follow. Steal this idea: line up the one long job you keep postponing, a market scan or a migration, so it's ready the day access opens.

Second, the open-weights answer. Mistral released Large 4, a one-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, with weights on Hugging Face under a modified MIT license. API pricing is seventy cents per million input tokens and two dollars ten per million output. Mistral says it scores forty-eight percent on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. Steal this idea: swap it into your favorite coding agent for an afternoon and compare cost per finished task.

Third, the creator's crew. Riverside launched four agents: a Producer, an Editor, a Clipper and a Marketer. They take a recording from prep to published clips, strip pauses and filler, add captions and branding, and schedule posts. Nothing publishes without the creator's approval, and they're included in every plan. Steal this idea: feed one long webinar to the Clipper and count the minute-long highlights.

Fourth, Canva Brush. A vision-language model that restyles a slide or a whole deck from one prompt. Canva says it's up to sixty-nine percent faster and forty-six percent cheaper per edit than its previous design agent. It's in Canva AI for Pro subscribers from October twenty-ninth. Steal this idea: take your best campaign graphic and remix it for four channels in one pass.

And fifth, the lab one. Anthropic reports results from six research partners. Generate Biomedicines used Claude Code to redesign a CAR T-cell signaling domain that came out about seventy percent shorter, with roughly ten times as many surface receptors. BigHat Biosciences tested about a thousand antibody variants in ten weeks. And Enveda cut manufacturing-document review by eighty-nine percent. Over twenty-five hours, down to under three. Steal this idea: pick one slow review in a lab and time it against Claude. That's the launch pad. Handing it back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Lena, what broke through the noise this week?

segments.speaker: social_correspondent
segments.text: Jordan, a few things stopped the scroll. Let me start with a Reel about robots.

segments.speaker: social_correspondent
segments.text:
Roberto Nickson, posting as rpn, made a Reel arguing that Genie four matters for robots, not just games. Google DeepMind's Genie four generates interactive worlds with native audio and dialogue that you steer in real time. It's a research preview for trusted testers, with Google AI Ultra subscribers next. His point: machines can practice millions of times in generated worlds before they touch the real one. This hit different because it turned a game demo into a rehearsal room. Steal this idea: describe one process you run, a loading dock, a test rig, a customer visit, and watch what the rehearsal gets wrong.

Second, Instagram started testing Features on October twenty-sixth. Horizontal videos up to ninety minutes, for podcasts, interviews and full shows. Creators can cut Reels from a Feature that link back to the full video. It starts with select US creators and some in Brazil. Creators were already planning: record one long video, post the best sixty seconds as Reels. One Reel says up to eight clips can point to a single Feature. Short clip as trailer, long video as the product. Steal this idea: record one long demo, mark eight moments that work alone, and you've got a month of posts from one session.

Third, and my pick for anyone who works with materials. The University of Nottingham's coatings group built a self-driving lab with two robotic arms and a liquid-dispensing tool. It prepares a precursor solution, runs the furnace, controls cooling and retrieves the sample. The target is heat-resistant thermal barrier coatings. AI active learning helped identify and prepare several candidate pyrochlore materials, in a paper in Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence. A robot that never gets bored. Steal this idea: map one formulation-and-cure workflow your lab repeats every week, and ask which steps an arm and a scheduler could take. Lena Park, signing off. Back to the desk, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Lena just showed us a robotic coatings lab. Dr. Vogel, the research desk has the science, and a pick for the skeptics.

segments.speaker: research_correspondent
segments.text:
Thank you, Jordan. Lena's Nottingham robots have a neighbor on my desk, and I'll save the reality check for the end. Let's start with a result that genuinely made me sit up. Linköping University, in the journal Science. The team used machine learning to mine historical reports and flagged thirty-three previously made but unrecognized MXenes, a family of two-dimensional materials. Guided by that list, they made seven multilayer MXenes with a self-propagating high-temperature method. It needs no sustained external heating and finishes within minutes. They also made eleven brand-new rare-earth MXenes. Old literature was hiding materials that had already been made. Steal this idea: point a language model at two hundred papers from your own corner, say cements, insulation foams or coatings. Pull compound and process into a table. Then look for combinations made once and never followed up.

A second, quicker one. In a paper from the Institute of Science Tokyo, language-model agents assessed one another's work on an ensemble of quantum spins in diamond. Repeated reference measurements showed the signal was drifting, so the agents called the first run inconclusive and revised the protocol without loosening the acceptance criteria. The revised run supported the theory. A reviewer agent that can say no turns a lab agent from a fast typist into a colleague. Steal this idea: take one routine measurement, a tensile test log or a sensor calibration, let one agent propose the analysis, and have a second try to break it.

Now, this week's share-this-with-your-lab pick. A Nature Synthesis paper on perovskite solar cells. The team combined retrosynthetic prediction, density functional theory screening and chemical expertise to rank molecules for the interface layer. More than ninety thousand structures, built from three hundred eight fragments, narrowed to three hundred candidates scored on eight descriptors. The top molecule, called AI-one, took devices to twenty-seven point two percent power-conversion efficiency. And they kept more than ninety-five percent of initial efficiency after two thousand hours of maximum-power-point tracking at sixty-five degrees Celsius. Here's why a skeptical chemist should care. The ranking blends interface descriptors with synthetic accessibility, so the shortlist is something a bench can actually make. And the screening code is public on GitHub. The same screen-by-makeability pattern applies to coatings, binders and interface layers. Here's how I'd put it in front of a lab. Clone the repository. Swap in twenty fragments from one of your own coating or adhesion problems. Then compare its top ten against what your chemists would have picked by hand. Make that side-by-side the next group-meeting demo.

Now, the reality check. Three quick ones. First, a study of nine research agents on fifteen problems. About four in five unsupported numbers in AI-written papers came from the wrong run or the wrong metric, not from invention. A claim-to-evidence checker certified claims with over ninety percent precision. An AI verifier recovered more traceable claims but accepted about three times as many misattributed ones, so the authors say the two work best together. Second, OpenAI describes a four-layer system that monitors every reinforcement-learning run, evaluation and tool-using harness for models at least as capable as GPT-six Astra. It says the highest-priority security alerts reach responders typically within fifteen minutes. Third, Colorado held its hearing on automated-decision and chatbot rules on October twenty-sixth. Final rules are due before January first, twenty twenty-seven, when both laws take effect. The interim draft and the regulatory analysis are on the Attorney General's page. With that, back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Here's what I'd try this week. For fun: put four phones on a table and play air hockey across all of them. For the weekend: feed one long recording to a clipper and see how many minute-long highlights come back. And for the lab: clone the perovskite screening code, swap in twenty fragments from a coating problem of your own, and put the top ten next to your chemists' picks.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Next week, watch for three openings. Tomorrow, Project ProtoStar opens its first challenge, running November second through thirteenth. Hugging Face and its university partners, with Carnegie Mellon hosting, want predictions of temperature, precipitation, hottest day and cooling degree days for two hundred ten US cities. Anyone can enter, and cooling degree days map straight onto building energy. Second, expert groups are examining OpenAI's three claimed results in math, computer science and physics, including a group led by David Gross. The math and computer science proofs are public. And third, Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard, a research preview co-developed with HHMI Janelia, which lets agents operate lab instruments. Three doors, all open soon.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: That's your week. Full breakdown, every link, every source — at the AI Brief Hub. I'm Jordan Reeves. Back next Sunday.
